title: To-morrow's a new day
paragraphs: I give, as it seems to me, with good reason the palm to Jacques Amyot above all our French writers — not only for the simplicity and purity of his language, in which he excels all others, nor for his perseverance in carrying through so long a work, nor for the depth of his learning that allowed him to smooth out and untangle so knotty and intricate an author so successfully (for whatever people say, I know nothing of Greek; but I meet with a sense so well held together and sustained throughout his whole translation that he must either have known the true mind of the author, or, by long acquaintance with him, imprinted a vivid and general idea of Plutarch in his soul — for he has given us nothing that detracts from or contradicts him); but above all I am most taken with him for having so well chosen a book so worthy and so useful to present to his country. We ignorant fellows would have been lost if this book had not raised us out of the dirt; by his favour we now dare speak and write; the ladies are able to instruct schoolmasters; it is our breviary. If this good man is still alive, I would commend Xenophon to him to do as much for that author; it is a much easier task than the other, and consequently fitter for his age. And besides, though I cannot say quite how, it seems to me he trips briskly and clearly enough over steps another would have stumbled at, yet still his style seems more his own where he does not meet those difficulties, and rolls along at his ease.

I was just now reading the passage where Plutarch says of himself that Rusticus, being present at a declamation of his in Rome, received a packet from the emperor and put off opening it until everything was over — for which, he says, the whole company highly praised that man's gravity. True enough, given that he was on the subject of curiosity and that eager passion for news which makes us, with so much indiscretion and impatience, drop everything to attend to a newcomer and tear open on the spot, no matter what company we are in, the letters delivered to us — he had reason to applaud Rusticus's gravity in this instance, and he might further have added the commendation of his civility and courtesy in not interrupting the flow of his declamation. But I doubt whether anyone can commend his prudence: with unexpected letters, especially from an emperor, putting off reading them might have done great harm. The vice opposite to curiosity is negligence, to which I naturally incline, and in which I have seen some men so extreme that one might find letters sent them three or four days before still sealed in their pockets.

I never open any letters addressed to another — not only those entrusted to me, but even those that fortune has steered into my hand. I am cross with myself if my eyes unintentionally pick up any contents from letters of importance that a great man is reading while I stand near him. Never was a man less inquisitive or less prying into other men's affairs than I.

In our fathers' time, Monsieur de Boutières nearly lost Turin by having, while in good company at supper, put off reading information sent to him of the treason plotted against that city, which he commanded. And this same Plutarch has informed me that Julius Caesar would have saved himself if, on his way to the Senate the day he was assassinated by the conspirators, he had read a note handed to him on the way. He also tells the story of Archias, the tyrant of Thebes, who, the night before the design Pelopidas had plotted to kill him and restore his country to liberty was executed, was sent a full written account of the whole conspiracy by another Archias, an Athenian; and this packet having been delivered to him while he sat at supper, he put off opening it, saying — what afterwards became a proverb in Greece — "Business tomorrow."

A wise man may, I think, out of consideration for another — so as not to disturb the company, as Rusticus did, or break off some important business in hand — defer reading or hearing some new thing brought to him; but to defer for his own interest or private pleasure, especially if he is a public minister, refusing to interrupt his dinner or break his sleep, is inexcusable. There was anciently at Rome the so-called "consular place" at the table, which was the most honourable as being the freest, and most accessible to those who came in to speak with the person seated there. From which it appears that, even at meals, they did not entirely abandon the concern of other affairs and incidents. But when all is said, it is very hard in human actions to give so exact a rule on moral grounds that fortune will not still maintain her own right within it.
